newsitem.title: CHINA: HSBC opens Shanghai Pudong branch.
newsitem.headline: HSBC opens Shanghai Pudong branch.

text.p: The Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corp Ltd (HSBC) on Monday formally opened its branch in the Pudong area of Shanghai, and bank officials said they envisaged eventually moving its headquarters to the booming Chinese city.

The opening of HSBC's Pudong office put an official stamp of approval on the bank's local currency renminbi business and marked an important step in its strategy to be a major player in China's growing financial markets, said bank chairman John Strickland.
"China business is a strategically important part of the HSBC Group," Strickland said at the office's opening ceremony. "We can now offer services in renminbi through our new offices in Pudong."
The bank already has many customers asking about renminbi business, said Eddie Wang, chief executive officer of the bank's China operations.
"We have been encouraged by the large numbers of enquiries," Wang said. "We have had a very good start."
Wang declined to give details of the bank's renminbi deposits and loans, but said HSBC would start reducing reliance on the interbank market for local currency funds.
"The number one priority is to get more deposits," Wang said.

China has restricted the scope of local currency business for foreign financial institutions to the Shanghai area, and requires that banks set up an office in Pudong as a condition of handling renminbi transactions.
China would likely allow foreign banks to do renminbi business in other cities if the experiment in Shanghai proves successful, Strickland said.
Granting foreign banks a greater role in China's financial sector could eventually prompt the Hong Kong-based bank to move their headquarters to Shanghai, Strickland said.
"In time we want to put the headquarters here in Shanghai, but probably not just now," Strickland said, adding that China still had many restrictions on foreign financial bodies.
The Hongkong Bank was always headquartered in Hong Kong, although in pre-communist times before 1949, the Shanghai branch was much bigger and more important.
Strickland said most rules binding foreign financial business were intended to protect China's own banking sector, which is struggling to cope with market reform.
"We don't have complete freedom to act here in the way we have been able to in Hong Kong," he said.
Strickland said China would further open its financial sector after it felt its banking industry was ready to compete with big international financial firms.
"As soon as China and Shanghai are ready to create a level playing field, Shanghai will grow into a very important international financial centre," he said.
